strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem in brain-to-text NLP: overlapping subjects, repeated stimuli, and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate claims about generalization to unseen people and language.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is conceptually appropriate for the stated generalization target. The graph illustrations help explain why splitting individual observations can preserve unwanted dependencies.

The experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two established models, with additional-test-set and shuffled-input controls. Table 6 also reports decoding without teacher forcing, providing some evidence that differences between splitting methods persist beyond that evaluation confound.
weaknesses: The central benchmark still uses teacher forcing during evaluation. Table 6 identifies the scores reproduced in Tables 3–5 as teacher-forced results, meaning that even the proposed 'fair benchmark' exposes reference prefixes rather than measuring autonomous generation. The additional-test-set and shuffled-input controls are not repeated without teacher forcing. Table 6 partially addresses this issue, but does not establish whether the reported insensitivity to brain signals persists during free generation.

The published splitting algorithms do not enforce the promised guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership but can restore an edge connecting a training subject to a held-out text. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks story membership but can restore an edge involving a held-out subject. These conditions contradict the simultaneous constraints in Equations 13–14. Corrected algorithms and verification of pairwise train/validation/test disjointness are necessary to substantiate the benchmark.

Metric definitions and numerical reporting require an audit. Equation 17 counts intersections of individual brain signals, although the leakage definition concerns shared subject identity. Table 5 reports EEG2Text ROUGE-1 F=25.74 above both P=23.95 and R=23.98, which is inconsistent with standard F1 aggregation. Table 7 labels 40.65 as recall, whereas Table 3 labels the corresponding result as F1. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the quantitative conclusions.

The experiments do not establish several causal claims. Section 5.2 interprets decreasing validation loss on overlapping subjects as proof of overfitting and degraded representations; those curves alone cannot demonstrate deterioration on unseen subjects. Encoders should be compared on a common independent evaluation set. Comparisons across splitting methods also change training-data retention and subject/story composition, requiring controls before performance differences can be attributed entirely to leakage.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the claimed benchmark release. Appendix B provides useful hyperparameters and preprocessing references, but the manuscript does not provide exact retained sample counts, discarded-data proportions, split memberships, the additional test set's construction, or a link to code and split artifacts. The shuffling operation also needs a precise definition. Decoding results lack uncertainty across runs or subject/story partitions; four-seed reporting is provided only for leakage metrics.

The universal framing exceeds the supported scope. The proposed criterion evaluates joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli; shared-stimulus cross-subject evaluation can legitimately measure a different, explicitly restricted target. Claims that all current splitting methods are wrong, that evaluation becomes meaningless whenever overlap exists, and that leakage necessarily makes decoders ignore brain signals should be narrowed. The methodological motivation is worthwhile, but the evaluation, algorithmic, and reporting issues require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
